diagnosis: With the paragraph in its notes, the model still makes two main mistakes. First, when the seller states a cost below every listed price, it often offers the second-cheapest price instead of the cheapest, and when the stated cost is at or above the resale value it sometimes offers exactly the cost, which loses money because the seller accepts. The long chain of 'equal to the cost, else cheapest above, never add a coin' clauses seems to confuse it. Second, when no cost is stated it often offers far too little, even below the lowest possible farm cost, where every offer is refused. The revision drops the 'add a coin' wording and gives the stated-cost case as one two-step check (lowest price not below the cost, and offer it only if it is under the resale value, otherwise the cheapest). It also says outright that offers below the lowest possible cost are always refused, and it puts the no-cost target as 'halfway between' the lowest cost and the resale value, capped at the highest possible cost.
method: Ignore usual market prices and ignore driving a hard bargain. If the seller states the farm cost, believe it and ignore the cost limits. Find the lowest listed price that is not below the cost; the seller accepts it. If the cost is below every listed price, this is the cheapest listed price. If this price is less than the resale value, offer it. If not, offer the cheapest listed price. If no cost is stated, any offer below the lowest possible farm cost is always refused. Find the number halfway between the lowest possible farm cost and the resale value, and round it down. If it is above the highest possible farm cost, use that highest cost instead. Offer the listed price equal to that number. If every listed price is above it, offer the cheapest; if every listed price is below it, offer the dearest.
